results.name: Required sections present
results.criterion: The lesson has an H2 section for each of: what is RAG, why it matters, how it works, a worked example, limits, recap, a self-check quiz, and key words.

results.name: Short sentences
results.criterion: Average sentence length <= 15 words AND no sentence longer than 25 words.
evidence: (30 words) It is a type of AI called a large language model (an LLM is an AI model trained on a very large amount of text to predict and generate language).
(26 words) Search: When you ask a question, the system converts your question into an embedding and searches the database to find the top few most similar chunks.
(28 words) The prompt sent to the AI looks like this: "Answer the user question using only this text chunk: [Chunk text: Exam fee last date is 15th July].
results.fix: Split every sentence longer than 25 words into two or three short sentences. One idea per sentence.

results.name: Plain-English readability
results.criterion: Flesch Reading Ease >= 60 on the lesson prose.

results.name: Right length for one sitting
results.criterion: Between 850 and 1800 words (~10-15 minutes of reading for a slow reader).

results.name: Self-check with answers
results.criterion: The quiz section has at least 3 questions and gives the answers.

results.name: Verified links to learn more
results.criterion: A 'Learn more' section links 2-4 resources, at least one a video, and EVERY link in the lesson is on the list verified live during research (no invented or broken URLs).

results.name: No false or misleading claims
results.criterion: Every technical claim agrees with the reference facts. No listed misconception is stated or implied as true. Simplifications are allowed only if they do not create a wrong belief (e.g. 'the model learns your documents' is a FAIL, because RAG does not change the model).
results.reasoning: I checked all forty specific statements and claims against the provided reference facts and misconceptions list. Every single technical statement, definition, and limitation description is completely accurate and avoids all listed misconceptions. Every technical claim in the lesson was thoroughly verified against the reference facts and misconceptions list. All descriptions of LLMs, embeddings, vector databases, RAG steps, limits, and definitions are completely accurate and free of misleading statements or overclaims.

results.name: All must-cover points taught
results.criterion: Every must-cover point in the reference is actually taught (explained, not just named).
results.reasoning: I checked every single must-cover item (M1 through M9) against the lesson text. All nine points are clearly explained with matching sections and explicit definitions, fully satisfying the requirements of the check.

results.name: Every technical term explained
results.criterion: Every technical or English-uncommon term is explained in simple words at or before its first use in the body (a glossary at the end alone does not count). Acronyms are expanded on first use.
results.reasoning: I checked every technical and uncommon term used in the lesson body. Every single term (like LLM, chunk, embedding, vector index, hallucination, prompt, retrieval, augmented, generation, and database) is defined clearly right at or before its first appearance.

results.name: Concrete analogy and walk-through
results.criterion: The lesson has (a) at least one everyday analogy a young Indian learner would recognise, correctly mapped to RAG, AND (b) one concrete worked example that follows a single question through every step: preparing documents, retrieving, adding to the prompt, generating.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for an everyday analogy suitable for a young Indian learner (an open-book college exam), verified its mapping to RAG, and checked the walk-through section. The walk-through explicitly covers document preparation (collecting, chunking, embedding, and storing), retrieval for a specific question, prompt construction with retrieved text, and final generation by the LLM.

results.name: Fits a non-native English beginner
results.criterion: Uses common, everyday English words; no idioms, slang, sarcasm or culturally obscure references; assumes no coding, maths beyond class 12, or prior AI knowledge; tone is encouraging and direct.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for idioms, overly complex or formal words, assumed knowledge of coding or advanced mathematics, grammar issues, and tone. The language used is simple, direct, avoids idioms, explains all technical terms it introduces, contains correct grammar, and consistently speaks to the reader as 'you' with an encouraging tone suitable for a beginner.

results.name: Builds step by step
results.criterion: Ideas are introduced before they are used; sections go from what -> why -> how -> example -> limits -> recap; each section links to the previous one; nothing is repeated without purpose.
results.reasoning: The lesson strictly follows the required section order, introduces all technical terms before using them, maintains a smooth flow between sections without abrupt transitions, and uses analogies purposefully right where concepts are introduced.
